title: Full Irish Breakfast
subtitle: Bacon, sausage, white pudding, egg, and soda bread
excerpt: Ireland's cooked breakfast, with its own distinctive cast of characters: back bacon, pork sausages, white pudding, and a slice of soda bread alongside.
sourceNotes: Traditional Irish cooked breakfast, known in Ireland simply as a 'fry'. White pudding (a pork and oat sausage without blood) and soda bread are the distinguishing elements from an English or Scottish fry.

recipe.temperatureNote: Oven temperature for keeping cooked items warm while the plate comes together

glossaryTerms.definition: To melt fat slowly out of meat over moderate heat, which crisps it and releases flavour into the pan.
In Irish usage, 'a fry' refers to the full cooked breakfast itself, the complete plate rather than just a cooking method.

content.text: A full Irish breakfast, called simply a
fry

in Ireland, is its own creature, distinct from its English and Scottish cousins. White pudding stands in alongside or instead of black, the bacon is often thicker and milder, and a slice of soda bread arrives at the side rather than shop-bought toast. It gives you a deeply satisfying plate with a gentler richness than the Scottish version. Getting everything hot and ready at the same moment is the challenge; a low oven to hold cooked items is the solution.
What you need

items.prepNote: white pudding if available, otherwise black pudding, cut into 1 cm slices

content.text: Fry the meats
Heat the oven to 180 °C and put the baking tray in to warm. Place the large frying pan over medium heat with 10 g of the butter. Add the
sausages-pork
and cook for 10 to 12 minutes, turning regularly until golden brown all over and cooked through. Move them to the warm tray in the oven.
Lay the
back-bacon
rashers in the same pan over medium-high heat. Let the fat
render

for 2 minutes per side, Irish back bacon is thicker than streaky, so it needs a little longer. Transfer to the oven. Add the pudding slices to the pan; 2 minutes per side is all they need. The outside firms and colours without extra fat. Add to the oven.
Add another 10 g butter to the pan. Cook the
mushrooms-button
over medium heat for 4 minutes, turning once. Set the
tomato
halves in cut-side down alongside for 3 minutes until softened and starting to caramelise. Season and move both to the oven.
Cook the eggs
Set the small frying pan over medium-low heat with the remaining butter. Crack the
eggs
in gently and cook for 2 to 3 minutes. The whites should set fully while the yolks stay soft. Spoon a little of the hot butter over the whites if they are slow to set. Season with a pinch of salt.
Build the plate

Warm two plates if you can, a cold plate cools everything fast. Arrange the sausages, bacon, pudding, mushrooms, and tomato, then lay the egg alongside. Serve with a thick slice of soda bread on the side and, if using, a small pot of warmed baked beans. In Ireland, brown sauce is the traditional accompaniment rather than ketchup, though either works.
Troubleshooter

Sausages splitting open during cooking: the heat is too high. Irish-style sausages have a high pork content and a delicate skin, a medium heat and patient turning prevents them bursting. Never prick them; it just lets the fat escape.

Everything arrives at different temperatures: put the thickest items (sausages, bacon) in first and work through to the fastest-cooking items last. The oven hold is not optional, skip it and the first things you cooked will be cold by the time the eggs are done.
Where this dish lives

The full Irish breakfast is called a 'fry' in everyday speech and is served from Donegal to Cork, in farmhouse B&Bs, hotel dining rooms, and the kind of no-frills café where the tea comes in a pot and the bread is made fresh that morning. White pudding is the element most visitors find surprising, a pale, milder relative of black pudding made from pork, oatmeal, and spices without the blood. It is a staple in every Irish butcher and the item that makes the plate distinctly Irish. Soda bread on the side is not a garnish; it's there to mop up the yolk and the bacon fat, and it earns its place.
